statement: EBITDA is one of the most popular and widely used GAAP KPIs; it is regulated by IAS 1.
explanation: Wrong. EBITDA is very popular but it is a NON-GAAP measure: no IFRS standard defines or requires it, and companies calculate it differently (e.g. treatment of leases, provisions, non-recurring items). Under IFRS 18 such subtotals will be 'management-defined performance measures' requiring a reconciliation – but still not defined by IFRS.

statement: EBITDA differs from the net cash flow from operations in the cash flow statement in that it is before adjustments for working capital changes.
explanation: Correct. Operating cash flow ≈ EBITDA − change in working capital needs − income tax paid (± other non-cash items). EBITDA is only an approximation of the cash generated by operations because it ignores the cash tied up in inventories and receivables (or released through payables) and the taxes paid (Inditex example).

statement: EBITDA is often used when valuing a company; it helps to compare companies with different financial structures, different depreciation policies and different tax rates.
explanation: Correct. EBITDA is before interest (neutralises the debt/equity mix), before taxes (neutralises tax rates) and before depreciation/amortisation (neutralises useful lives and methods). That is why it is used in multiples (EV/EBITDA) and debt covenants (net debt/EBITDA). Its weakness: it ignores the capital intensity of the business.

statement: ROCE measures how a company performs in using shareholders' capital to generate earnings.
explanation: Wrong. ROCE relates operating profit after tax (NOPAT = EBIT × (1 − t)) to CAPITAL EMPLOYED = equity + net financial debt (or non-current assets + working capital needs) – i.e. the capital provided by BOTH shareholders and lenders. The return on shareholders' capital is ROE = net income / equity.

statement: Considering ROCE = EBIT × (1 − t) / capital employed, ROCE is not affected by depreciation policies.
explanation: Wrong. EBIT is calculated AFTER depreciation and amortisation, and capital employed contains the net carrying amount of non-current assets – both depend on useful lives and methods. Longer useful lives raise EBIT and capital employed (e.g. Lufthansa 20 years vs. Ryanair 23 years with 15% residual value), so comparisons need adjustments.

statement: A company can improve ROCE by deferring profitable investments (e.g. in PP&E), but this strategy may reduce the firm's value.
explanation: Correct. Postponing capex keeps capital employed low (and old, largely depreciated assets) → ROCE rises in the short run. But if the investments would have earned more than the WACC, deferring them destroys value (EVA). ROCE alone can be manipulated by under-investment.

statement: Using an 'asset' approach to calculate capital employed, working capital needs equal current assets minus current liabilities.
explanation: Wrong. Working capital NEEDS are operating items only: inventories + trade receivables − trade payables. Cash and short-term financial debt are excluded, because they are part of net financial debt (financing side). Capital employed = net non-current assets + working capital needs = equity + net financial debt.

statement: The only way to increase ROCE is to increase the NOPAT margin.
explanation: Wrong. DuPont: ROCE = NOPAT margin (NOPAT/sales) × capital employed turnover (sales/capital employed). ROCE can also be increased by using capital more efficiently: higher sales with the same assets, faster inventory and receivables turnover, longer payables, disposal of unused assets.

statement: Dividends paid to shareholders reduce the free cash flow to the firm.
explanation: Wrong. FCF to the firm = operating cash flow − net capex: it is the cash available to ALL capital providers BEFORE any payments to them. Dividends (and debt repayments) are financing flows that USE the free cash flow; they do not reduce it.

statement: Debt repayments do not reduce the free cash flow to the firm, but they reduce the free cash flow to equity.
explanation: Correct. FCFE = FCF to the firm + net increase in financial debt − financial expenses × (1 − t). Repaying debt lowers the net debt increase and therefore the cash left for shareholders, while FCFF is unaffected.

statement: EVA can be improved by decreasing the WACC.
explanation: Correct. EVA = NOPAT − WACC × capital employed = (ROCE − WACC) × capital employed. A lower cost of capital (e.g. cheaper financing, lower risk) increases EVA, as do a higher NOPAT or less capital for the same NOPAT.

statement: Non-GAAP financial indicators are indicators whose disclosure is mandatory under IFRS.
explanation: Wrong. Non-GAAP (alternative) performance measures are, by definition, NOT defined by any accounting regulation (e.g. EBITDA, free cash flow, ROCE, net debt). Companies publish them voluntarily; ESMA guidelines (and from 2027 IFRS 18 for MPMs) require definitions and reconciliations.

statement: Segment information, profit/loss from discontinued operations and earnings per share are GAAP KPIs when using IFRS.
explanation: Correct. They are required and defined by IFRS (IFRS 8, IFRS 5 and IAS 33). EBITDA, ROCE, FCF and EVA are non-GAAP.

statement: If two companies have the same EBITDA and capital employed but Company B has a higher amortisation expense, B's ROCE is lower than C's.
explanation: Correct. Higher amortisation → lower EBIT → lower NOPAT for the same capital employed → lower ROCE.

statement: Free cash flow to the firm equals free cash flow to equity when the company has no debt.
explanation: Correct. Without financial debt there are no net borrowings and no interest, so all free cash flow belongs to shareholders.

statement: Reducing clients' payment terms improves a negative EBITDA.
explanation: Wrong. Payment terms affect working capital and cash flow, not EBITDA. To improve EBITDA a company must raise operating revenues or cut cash operating costs (e.g. cost of raw materials consumed). Lower depreciation does not change EBITDA (it is added back), and reducing debt only affects interest below EBITDA (exam 2024).

prompt: W.Com reported a negative EBITDA. Which alternative would improve EBITDA?

options.text: Decrease the cost of raw materials consumed

explanation: Only operating income/expenses above depreciation affect EBITDA. Depreciation is added back, interest is below EBITDA, payment terms only affect working capital.

options.text: that are confidential but audited by the company's auditors
that are not defined by any accounting regulation
whose disclosure is mandatory according to IFRS
whose disclosure is mandatory according to stock market regulation if the company is listed

explanation: EBITDA, FCF, ROCE, EVA, net debt… are not defined by IFRS. Market regulators (ESMA) set rules on how they are presented, but do not make them mandatory (exam 2024).

prompt: Regarding Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) it is correct to say that …

options.text: it indicates how successful the company was in generating returns for shareholders
it is a KPI rarely published by listed companies
it is calculated as operating profit divided by capital employed
it is calculated as EBITDA divided by total assets
it is mandatory to present ROCE in an IFRS annual report

explanation: ROCE = operating profit (EBIT, often after tax: NOPAT) / capital employed. Returns to shareholders = ROE. ROCE is non-GAAP but frequently published (exam 2023).

prompt: Regarding Free Cash Flow it is correct to say that …

options.text: it is calculated as operating profit minus cash outflows for investments
it has to be presented in the cash flow statement according to IAS 1 and IAS 7
it is a non-GAAP KPI that is frequently published by listed companies
it indicates the cash available to shareholders for dividends

explanation: FCF to the firm = operating CASH FLOW (not operating profit) − net capex; it is not defined by IAS 7 and belongs to all capital providers (exam 2019).

Which KPI is calculated in the excerpt, and what does it show?

options.text: Free cash flow to the firm – cash available to all capital providers after investments
Free cash flow to equity – cash available after debt service

explanation: Operating cash flow − investing cash flow = FCF to the firm: 2,882 in 2022 (cash to repay debt or pay shareholders) vs −920 in 2021 (investments exceeded operating cash, financed externally).

prompt: Operating profit is 4,357 m€, depreciation and amortisation 1,100 m€, operating cash flow 4,029 m€. What is EBITDA?
explanation: EBITDA = operating profit + depreciation & amortisation = 4,357 + 1,100. The operating cash flow is a distractor.

prompt: EBITDA 1,000; depreciation and amortisation 200; average capital employed 4,000. Ignoring taxes, what is ROCE?
Equity 20 m€, financial debt 140 m€, provisions 20 m€, cash 10 m€. What is capital employed (equity + net financial debt)?
explanation: Net financial debt = 140 − 10 = 130; capital employed = 20 + 130 = 150. Provisions are excluded in this simple liability approach (mock exam).

prompt: EBIT 1,000 m€; D&A 100; tax rate 25%; increase in working capital needs 80; capex 800. What is FCF to the firm?

F has a NOPAT margin of 5% and a capital employed turnover of 2.0. Competitor G: EBIT × (1 − t) 990; sales 9,000; capital employed 12,000. Compared with F, G has …

options.text: a higher NOPAT margin and a lower capital employed turnover
a lower margin and a higher turnover
a higher margin and a higher turnover

explanation: G: margin 11%, turnover 0.75 → ROCE 8.25% vs F 10%. Different business models: G earns more per € of sales, F uses its capital more intensively.

prompt: How can capital employed be determined?

options.text: Net non-current assets + working capital needs (asset approach), or equity + net financial debt (liability approach)
Net non-current assets only, without working capital

explanation: Asset side: net non-current assets (non-current assets − other non-current liabilities) + working capital needs (inventories + receivables − payables). Liability side: equity + net financial debt (long- and short-term financial debt − cash). On a reformulated balance sheet both give the same amount; capital employed can be taken at year-end or as the average of two years. Total assets or equity alone are not capital employed.

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a critical point when comparing KPIs between companies?

options.text: Different accounting policies (FIFO vs WAC, depreciation methods)
Different estimates such as useful lives and residual values
Different definitions of the same KPI
The colour of the annual report

explanation: E.g. Lufthansa depreciates aircraft over 20 years (5% residual value), Ryanair over 23 years (15%) – analysts adjust such differences before comparing.

prompt: Which KPI is calculated in the excerpt? Explain its calculation and meaning, and comment on 2021 and 2022.
modelAnswer: It is the free cash flow to the firm: net cash flow from operating activities − net cash flow used in investing activities (net capex). 2022: 5,168 − 2,286 = 2,882; 2021: 199 − 1,119 = −920. FCFF shows the cash generated by operations after the investments needed to maintain/expand capacity, available to repay debt and remunerate shareholders. In 2022 the company generated substantial free cash flow; in 2021 operating cash flow did not cover investments, so the gap had to be financed by new debt, equity or cash reserves. FCF is a non-GAAP KPI.
keyPoints: Free cash flow to the firm = CFO − CFI (net capex)
Meaning: cash available to debt and equity holders
Interpretation of both years (financing need in 2021)

steps.title: Identify the KPI from its formula
steps.why: Operating cash flow minus investing cash flow = free cash flow to the firm (FCFF): cash generated by the business after the investments needed to maintain/expand capacity.
lines: FCFF = net CF from operating activities − net CF used in investing activities

steps.title: Interpret
steps.why: FCFF is the cash available to all capital providers (repay debt, pay interest and dividends). 2022: operations generated much more cash than was invested → strong position. 2021: operating cash flow did not cover investments → the gap of 920 had to be financed with new debt, equity or cash reserves (e.g. crisis year).

steps.title: Classify the KPI
steps.why: FCF is not defined by IFRS → non-GAAP indicator; definitions vary between companies.

pitfalls: Confusing FCFF with FCFE: FCFE also deducts net debt repayments/interest.

prompt: Calculate ABC's ROCE and EVA and interpret the result.
modelAnswer: NOPAT = 1,848 × (1 − 0.25) = 1,386 m€. ROCE = 1,386 / 32,780 = 4.2%. EVA = NOPAT − WACC × capital employed = 1,386 − 0.065 × 32,780 = 1,386 − 2,130.7 = −744.7 m€ (= (4.2% − 6.5%) × 32,780). The company earns less on its capital employed than its cost of capital: it is profitable in accounting terms but destroys economic value.

steps.title: NOPAT
steps.why: ROCE and EVA use the operating result after tax, independent of financing: EBIT × (1 − tax rate).

steps.title: Interpret
steps.why: ROCE (4.2%) < WACC (6.5%): ABC is profitable in accounting terms (positive net income) but earns less than its capital providers require → it destroys economic value.

pitfalls: Using EBITDA or profit after tax (1,181) instead of EBIT × (1 − t).
Multiplying WACC by sales or total assets instead of capital employed.

prompt: Explain the DuPont decomposition of ROCE and two ways to improve it.
modelAnswer: ROCE = EBIT(1 − t) / capital employed = [EBIT(1 − t) / sales] × [sales / capital employed] = NOPAT margin × capital employed turnover. The margin can be improved by higher prices or lower operating costs (expense analysis); the turnover by using capital more efficiently: higher sales per € of non-current assets, faster inventory and receivables turnover, longer payables, disposing of unused assets. Caution: cutting necessary investments may raise ROCE short-term but reduce value.
keyPoints: ROCE = NOPAT margin × capital employed turnover

steps.title: Lever 1 – NOPAT margin
steps.why: Earn more per € of sales: higher prices/better mix, lower cost of sales or operating expenses.

steps.title: Lever 2 – capital employed turnover
steps.why: Generate more sales per € of capital: better use of non-current assets, faster inventory and receivable turnover, longer payable terms, sale of unused assets.

steps.title: Caution
steps.why: Cutting necessary investments raises ROCE in the short term (smaller CE) but may destroy value in the long run.
steps.result: ROCE = margin × turnover; improve either lever

pitfalls: Using equity instead of capital employed (that would be ROE).

prompt: Calculate ROCE after tax for N and N−1, decompose it into NOPAT margin and capital employed turnover, and recompute ROCE N with operational profit (before non-recurring items).
keyPoints: With operational profit 7.22% – flattering, non-recurring items excluded

steps.title: Decompose
steps.why: The margin improved, but capital employed more than doubled (new leases and borrowings) while sales grew only 8% → turnover collapsed and ROCE fell.

steps.title: Management's version: operational profit
steps.why: Excluding 'non-recurring' expenses flatters ROCE. Acceptable only with a clear definition, a reconciliation to IFRS operating profit and consistency over time.

pitfalls: Using net income instead of operating profit after tax.
Forgetting lease debt in capital employed.
